To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
auditory and visual stimuli can both capture attention exogenously, but that the processing of subsequent auditory and visual stimuli is delayed when these stimuli belong to a different modality.

(a) attentional shifts between visual and auditory stimuli are possible; (b) attentional shifts from vision to audition are slower than from audition to vision; and (c) the processing of a visual stimulus is delayed when preceded by an auditory stimulus, but the processing of an auditory stimulus is not delayed by a visual stimulus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether attentional shifts between visual and auditory stimuli are possible without any spatial shift.
the role of attention in the perception of visual and auditory stimuli.
how the mind processes information from multiple sensory modalities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
attentional limitation is not limited to the visual modality but is a general phenomenon that can be observed in both vision and audition.
the processing of a stimulus in a particular modality depends on the modality of the previous stimulus.

auditory stimuli do not have a more automatic alerting function than visual stimuli, and that cross-modal attentional limitations are due to a combination of exogenous and endogenous attentional shifts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the attentional system is not only spatially but also modality dependent, and that the modality effect is not limited to the early sensory processing stage but can be observed in higher level attentional mechanisms.
the processing of a stimulus in one modality (e.g., vision) may be delayed by the processing of a simultaneous stimulus in another modality (e,g., audition).
the modality-specific attentional system is more flexible than previously thought, but the flexibility is limited by the modality of the stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the modality in which a stimulus is presented affects how we process subsequent stimuli.
the brain is not a general-purpose information-processing machine.
the modality in which an event is presented can affect the processing of a later stimulus in the same modality, and that this effect is not limited to spatial attention.
